Bayesian Inference, Markov Chains and Sampling

Handle uncertainty the way modern models do. Read joint, marginal and conditional distributions, measure distance with the multivariate normal, update beliefs with Bayes and conjugate priors, watch Markov chains settle, estimate with Monte Carlo, sample posteriors with Metropolis, and see how concentration inequalities guarantee how close an average is.

Part 1

🧩Joint, marginal and conditional distributions

Real data has several variables at once: the weather and whether people carry umbrellas, a patient’s age and blood pressure, a pixel and its neighbour. The joint distribution P(X, Y) gives the chance of every combination. From it you can get everything else.

🧮 Marginal (sum out the other variable)
P(X = x) = Σy P(X = x, Y = y)
Add across a row of the joint table. The name comes from writing these totals in the margin.
🧮 Conditional (zoom into one row or column)
P(Y = y | X = x) = P(X = x, Y = y)P(X = x)
Keep only the cases where X = x, then rescale so they add to 1.
🧮 Independence
P(X, Y) = P(X) P(Y) for every cell
Knowing X tells you nothing about Y. Then P(Y | X) = P(Y).
🔍 Going deeper: the chain rule of probability and why it matters

Rearranging the conditional formula gives the product rule: P(X, Y) = P(X) P(Y | X). Repeating it gives the chain rule of probability: P(x₁, x₂, …, xₙ) = P(x₁) P(x₂ | x₁) P(x₃ | x₁, x₂) ⋯ P(xₙ | x₁, …, xₙ₋₁).

This is exactly how a large language model scores a sentence. It predicts the first word, then the second word given the first, then the third given the first two, and multiplies (in practice, adds the logs of) all those conditional probabilities. Naive Bayes (Chapter 9) is the same chain rule with a bold simplification: it pretends the features are independent once the class is known.

For continuous variables, sums become integrals: p(x) = ∫ p(x, y) dy. The ideas do not change.

Generative models learn a joint distribution, for example p(image, label) or p(all the words of a text). Discriminative models such as logistic regression learn only the conditional p(label | image). Marginalising, summing out what you do not know, is at the heart of Bayesian inference and of mixture models.
Part 2

🥚The multivariate normal and Mahalanobis distance

The bell curve of Chapter 10 has a version for many variables at once, the multivariate normal. It is described by a mean vector μ (the centre) and a covariance matrix Σ (the spread of each variable and how pairs move together). Its contour lines, the points of equal density, are ellipses. The covariance matrix decides their shape and tilt, and its eigenvectors (Chapter 5) point along the axes of the ellipses.

🧮 Density of a d dimensional normal
p(x) = 1(2π)d/2 |Σ|1/2 exp(−½ (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ))
The part inside exp is minus half the squared Mahalanobis distance. |Σ| is the determinant.
🧮 Mahalanobis distance
dM(x) = √((x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ))
Distance measured in standard deviations, taking the shape of the data into account. With Σ = I it is the ordinary distance.
🔍 Going deeper: three facts that make the normal so useful

Linear maps keep it normal. If x ~ N(μ, Σ) then Ax + b ~ N(Aμ + b, AΣAᵀ). That is how samples are drawn: take independent standard normal z and form μ + Lz with LLᵀ = Σ (Cholesky, Chapter 13).

Marginals and conditionals stay normal. Any subset of the variables is normal, and so is any subset given the rest. The conditional mean is a straight line in the known values, which is one more reason linear regression is so natural.

Zero correlation means independence, but only for jointly normal variables. In general, uncorrelated variables can still depend on each other strongly, for example x and x² when x is symmetric around 0.

Gaussian discriminant analysis fits one multivariate normal per class. Anomaly detection flags points with a large Mahalanobis distance. Gaussian processes, Kalman filters and the noise in diffusion models are all built on the multivariate normal. The "reparameterisation trick" of variational autoencoders is exactly μ + σz.
Part 3

🪙Bayesian inference: priors, posteriors and MAP

Chapter 9 used Bayes’ rule for events. Bayesian inference uses it for an unknown parameter, such as the chance θ that a coin lands heads. Instead of one best guess, you keep a whole distribution of belief over θ and update it with data.

🧮 Bayes’ rule for a parameter
p(θ | data) = p(data | θ) · p(θ)p(data)   ∝   likelihood × prior
Prior: belief before the data. Likelihood: how well each θ explains the data. Posterior: updated belief. p(data) only rescales.

For a coin, a very convenient prior is the Beta distribution, Beta(a, b), whose density is proportional to θa − 1(1 − θ)b − 1. You can read a and b as "imaginary heads plus 1" and "imaginary tails plus 1". When the data are h heads and t tails, the posterior is again a Beta. A prior with this property is called conjugate.

🧮 Beta Binomial update
Beta(a, b) prior + h heads, t tails → Beta(a + h, b + t) posterior
Updating is just counting. The posterior mean is (a + h) ÷ (a + b + h + t).
EstimateRuleBeta(2, 2) prior, 7 heads in 10
MLE (maximum likelihood)the θ that makes the data most likely: h ÷ n0.700
MAP (maximum a posteriori)the peak of the posterior: (a + h − 1) ÷ (a + b + n − 2)8 ÷ 12 = 0.667
posterior mean(a + h) ÷ (a + b + n)9 ÷ 14 = 0.643
🔍 Going deeper: MAP is regularisation in disguise

Take logs: ln posterior = ln likelihood + ln prior + constant. Maximising the posterior (MAP) is therefore maximising the log likelihood plus a bonus from the prior.

Now put a normal prior on each weight of a model, w ~ N(0, σ²). Its log is −w² ÷ (2σ²) + constant. So MAP with a normal prior is exactly maximum likelihood with an L2 penalty, which is ridge regression or weight decay (Chapter 12). A Laplace prior, proportional to e−|w| ÷ b, gives the L1 penalty of lasso. A stronger belief that weights are small (smaller σ) means a stronger penalty.

With lots of data the likelihood dominates and MLE, MAP and the posterior mean all agree. With little data the prior matters, which is when it helps the most.

Bayesian ideas appear in A/B testing ("the chance B beats A is 94 %"), in spam filters, in Thompson sampling for recommendation systems, and in Bayesian optimisation for tuning hyperparameters. Bayesian neural networks keep a distribution over weights to say how unsure a prediction is.
A new restaurant with one 5 star review is not really better than one with 4.6 stars from 2000 reviews. Sensible ranking systems add a prior, some imaginary average reviews, so that a handful of ratings cannot jump to the top.
Part 4

🔁Markov chains and stationary distributions

A Markov chain moves between states at random, and the chance of the next state depends only on the current one, not on the history. Weather from day to day, a shopper moving between web pages and the next word in a very simple text model are common examples.

🧮 Transition matrix
Pᵢⱼ = P(next = j | now = i), each row adds up to 1
Row i lists where you can go from state i.
🧮 One step for a whole distribution
πt+1 = πt P
A row vector of probabilities times the matrix.
🧮 Stationary distribution
π = π P
Once reached, the distribution never changes. It is a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1 (Chapter 5).

A chain settles to one stationary distribution from any start when it is irreducible (every state can reach every other) and aperiodic (it does not cycle on a fixed rhythm). The "cycle" example in the animation fails the second condition and never settles.

Google’s original PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links, with a small chance of jumping to a random page so the chain is irreducible. Reinforcement learning is built on Markov decision processes, which are Markov chains with actions and rewards. MCMC, two lessons ahead, designs a chain whose stationary distribution is the distribution you want to sample.
Part 5

🎲Monte Carlo and inverse transform sampling

Monte Carlo methods answer questions by simulation. To find an average, a probability or an integral, draw many random samples and average the results. The law of large numbers makes the answer converge, and the central limit theorem (Chapter 11) says how fast.

🧮 Monte Carlo estimate
E[f(X)] ≈ 1n Σ f(xᵢ), with xᵢ drawn from X
An integral ∫₀¹ f(x) dx is E[f(U)] for a uniform U.
🧮 Its error
standard error = σ ÷ √n
Four times as many samples halve the error. This holds in any number of dimensions, which is why Monte Carlo wins in high dimensions.

Every simulation needs random numbers from the right distribution, but a computer only produces uniform numbers between 0 and 1. Inverse transform sampling converts them. If F is the CDF of the distribution you want, draw u uniformly and return x = F⁻¹(u). Values of x where F climbs steeply catch more of the u values, so they come out more often, exactly as they should.

🧮 Inverse transform
x = F⁻¹(u), u ~ Uniform(0, 1)
Exponential with rate λ: F(x) = 1 − e−λx, so x = −ln(1 − u) ÷ λ.
🔍 Going deeper: when the inverse is not available

For the normal distribution F⁻¹ has no simple formula. The Box Muller method turns two uniforms into two independent standard normals: √(−2 ln u₁) cos(2π u₂) and √(−2 ln u₁) sin(2π u₂).

Rejection sampling works for any density p you can evaluate. Choose an easy proposal q and a constant M with p ≤ M q everywhere. Draw x from q and keep it with probability p(x) ÷ (M q(x)). Kept points follow p exactly, but in high dimensions almost every point gets rejected.

Importance sampling keeps every point from q and gives it a weight p(x) ÷ q(x) instead. It is used in reinforcement learning to reuse old experience collected by an older policy.

Dropout at test time with many forward passes ("Monte Carlo dropout") estimates how unsure a network is. Policy gradient methods in reinforcement learning estimate gradients by averaging over sampled episodes. Diffusion models and VAEs sample noise with the methods of this lesson millions of times during training.
Part 6

⛓️MCMC and the Metropolis algorithm

Bayesian posteriors are often known only up to a constant: we can compute likelihood × prior, but not p(data), which needs an impossible integral. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) still produces samples. It builds a Markov chain that wanders through the parameter space and spends time in each region in proportion to its probability. The constant cancels out, so it is never needed.

  1. Start somewhere, at x.
  2. Propose a random nearby point x′, for example x plus a small random step.
  3. Compute the ratio r = p(x′) ÷ p(x). The unknown constant cancels in this ratio.
  4. Accept with probability min(1, r): always move uphill, sometimes move downhill. Otherwise stay at x (and count x again).
  5. Repeat many times, throw away the early "burn in" steps, and treat the rest as samples.
Step sizeWhat happensFix
too smallalmost every move is accepted, but the chain creeps and samples are strongly correlatedlarger steps
too largemost proposals land in low probability areas and are rejected, so the chain sits stillsmaller steps
about rightacceptance roughly 25 % to 50 %, and the chain explores welltune during burn in
Probabilistic programming tools such as Stan and PyMC fit Bayesian models with an advanced MCMC method called Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which uses gradients (from autodiff, Chapter 14) to make long, well aimed proposals. Simulated annealing, Gibbs sampling in topic models and energy based models are close relatives of Metropolis.
Metropolis in five words: propose, compare, accept or stay.
Part 7

📏Concentration inequalities and the law of large numbers

The law of large numbers says that the average of many independent samples gets close to the true mean. Concentration inequalities say how close, with a guarantee rather than an approximation. They are the mathematics behind "how much data is enough" and behind the theory of why machine learning generalises.

InequalityStatementNeeds
MarkovP(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] ÷ aX never negative
ChebyshevP(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1 ÷ k²a finite variance
Chebyshev for an averageP(|x̄ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ² ÷ (n ε²)independent samples
HoeffdingP(|x̄ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ 2 e−2nε²independent samples between 0 and 1
🔍 Going deeper: why this explains learning

A model’s error on the training set is an average over n examples. Its error on new data is the true mean. Hoeffding says that for one fixed model these are within ε of each other with probability at least 1 − 2e−2nε².

Training picks one model out of many, so the bound has to hold for all of them at once. With k possible models, adding up the failure chances (the union bound) gives probability at most 2k e−2nε². Solving for n shows that the data needed grows with ln k, the logarithm of the number of models. This is the core of PAC learning ("probably approximately correct"), and it is why a richer model family needs more data to avoid overfitting.

Concentration bounds decide how many users an A/B test needs, how many samples a Monte Carlo estimate needs, and how many rollouts a reinforcement learning agent needs. The ε greedy and UCB rules for multi armed bandits are built directly on Hoeffding’s inequality.
